A flat 6% and a reducing-balance 6%: compare the interest base and payment dates

Four charts compare original-principal flat interest with a monthly reducing-balance schedule, including payment components, principal allocation and a defined effective annual cash-flow equivalent.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare an original-principal interest quote with a reducing-balance quote

Interactive planning lab

Flat original-principal quote · monthly payment$466.67
Reducing-balance quote · monthly payment$443.21
Flat schedule · effective annual cash-flow equivalent11.71%

Two hypothetical fixed schedules advance the same principal at time zero and receive one payment at each month-end, starting one full month later. Flat interest equals original principal × flat annual quote × months / 12 and is divided equally across payments; allocated principal declines in equal amounts. The reducing-balance quote is nominal annual divided by twelve, charged to each month’s opening unpaid principal; the fixed payment amortizes it over the same number of months. Full-precision amounts are used, with only display rounding; these are mathematical schedules rather than cent-rounded lender invoices. The final reducing-balance payment closes floating-point residuals. The flat periodic equivalent solves advance = present value of the complete monthly payment schedule, then compounds that monthly rate for twelve months: (1 + monthly equivalent)^12 − 1. It is a defined effective annual cash-flow equivalent, not a jurisdiction-specific APR/EIR disclosure or legal-compliance test. At a zero advance the cost ratio is undefined and the headline stays N/A. Fees, insurance, taxes, defaults, early settlement, rebates and household funding are excluded. The principal chart is an allocation schedule, not a contractual early-payoff quote. All rate/term matrix cells use a normalized positive one-dollar advance, independently of selected loan size and quotes.

The central idea

A quoted percentage needs an interest base and a payment calendar. Compare the complete advance-and-repayment schedule before treating two headline rates as equivalent.

01

Identify the amount to which the interest rate applies

Two loan advertisements can display 6% while calculating interest on different amounts. One may keep using the original advance throughout the term; another may apply a monthly rate to the principal still unpaid at the beginning of each month.

This guide specifies both methods rather than treating “flat” as another name for fixed. A fixed rate describes whether a rate changes. An original-principal flat calculation describes its interest base. A reducing-balance loan can also have a fixed rate.

Singapore's official MoneySense explanation describes the distinction between flat interest on original principal and interest on a reducing balance. This article uses that conceptual distinction with its own hypothetical CAD advance, rates and payment schedule. It reproduces no provider offer or published loan example.

The two models share a CAD 10,000 advance at time zero and twenty-four payments, each received at a month-end. The first payment arrives after one complete month. Fees, insurance and other charges are excluded, allowing the rate-base calculation to be inspected separately.

02

Calculate the original-principal flat schedule explicitly

At a 6% annual flat quote over twenty-four months, total interest is CAD 10,000 × 6% × 24 ÷ 12 = CAD 1,200. Adding the advance gives CAD 11,200 of total scheduled repayments.

Dividing that total by twenty-four produces approximately CAD 466.67 per month. The unrounded mathematical payment is used throughout the calculator. Each payment allocates CAD 50 to interest and one twenty-fourth of the original advance to principal.

The flat-interest component stays at CAD 50 as the allocated unpaid principal falls. The formula continues to use the original CAD 10,000, rather than the amount still outstanding. A lower principal line therefore does not automatically create a lower flat-interest component.

Actual lenders may round installments to cents and adjust a final payment. This illustration rounds only what is displayed and does not claim that twenty-four rounded displayed payments will exactly reproduce an invoice. Obtain the contractual schedule for an actual repayment plan.

03

Apply the reducing rate to each opening principal balance

The comparison quote is a 6% nominal annual rate divided by twelve, or 0.5% per month. Its constant payment is chosen so twenty-four month-end payments fully amortize the same CAD 10,000 advance.

The mathematical payment is approximately CAD 443.21. Total interest over the schedule is approximately CAD 636.95, producing total repayments of approximately CAD 10,636.95. Both examples repay the same initial principal; their difference is the financing cost generated by the stated formulas.

The first month's interest is CAD 50 in both schedules because both initially use CAD 10,000 at a monthly 0.5%. Later reducing-balance interest falls because principal has been repaid. More of each fixed payment then goes toward principal.

The first chart compares selected monthly interest components. The principal chart shows why equal principal slices and equal amortizing payments create different allocation paths. Neither graph is an early-settlement quote: unearned-interest rebates, charges and actual payoff terms require the agreement.

04

Define the cash-flow equivalent before annualizing it

The flat quote's 6% is applied to the original amount, even while portions of that amount are being repaid. Dividing CAD 1,200 interest by CAD 10,000 and two years gives the stated flat rate, but that calculation does not value the timing of the monthly principal repayments.

The calculator instead solves for a monthly discount rate that makes the present value of all twenty-four flat-schedule payments equal to the CAD 10,000 received initially. There is one initial advance followed by positive repayments, so this fee-free schedule has a unique nonnegative periodic cost rate.

At the defaults, that monthly equivalent is approximately 0.92722%. Compounding its growth factor for twelve months produces an effective annual cash-flow equivalent of approximately 11.71%: (1 + monthly equivalent)12 − 1.

The reducing-balance quote's 0.5% monthly rate compounds to approximately 6.17% on the same annual basis. This article labels its convention explicitly. It does not assert that every jurisdiction's advertised EIR, APR or disclosure calculation uses that same annualization, or substitute the result for an actual required disclosure.

05

Use the term grid without assuming the flat quote simply doubles

The matrix repeats the flat-schedule calculation for different annual quotes and numbers of monthly payments. It uses a normalized positive one-dollar advance. Scaling both the advance and every repayment by the same amount leaves the periodic equivalent unchanged in this fee-free model.

The relationship between a flat quote and its effective annual cash-flow equivalent depends on the number and timing of payments. There is no universal rule that a flat rate should simply be doubled. The one-month and sixty-month columns show why the full schedule matters.

A zero flat quote produces zero interest and a zero equivalent cost rate. At a selected zero advance, however, there is no actual loan cash-flow ratio to infer. The headline reports N/A while the independent positive-unit matrix remains defined.

The comparison rates are separate editable inputs. A sufficiently low flat quote could produce a lower total payment than a higher reducing-balance quote. Comparing methods does not establish that one named structure always wins, and a payment that is lower per month can still run for a different period in an actual offer.

06

Reconcile a real offer in both dollars and dates

FCAC's personal-loan guide emphasizes understanding the total cost, including interest and fees, and comparing the payment amount over the stated number of payments. A complete comparison also needs the net amount actually received and the date of each outflow.

For a real quote, identify the original advance, any withheld or financed charges, the interest base, the rate's compounding convention and the exact payment calendar. Confirm what happens on an early settlement before using the remaining-principal line as an amount payable.

This example advances the full entered principal and charges no fees. A setup charge deducted before the borrower receives money changes the cash-flow equivalent even if the payment schedule is unchanged. A financed charge can also change principal and later interest. Those cases require their own complete schedule.

Finally, place the confirmed installments in the household budget. The model compares financing arithmetic; it calculates no income, available bank cash, credit approval or personal affordability. Equal annual headline rates are the beginning of the comparison, while an understandable dated repayment schedule makes the resulting obligation concrete.
